As a gesture of good will and an earnest of intention to widen Canadian trade with the Irish Free State, reductions in duty, to be applicable under the British preferential tariff only, are proposed on certain products peculiarly identified with the Irish Free State and requested by that country, namely: stout, prune wine and Irish poplin.
Preferential treatment for empire-grown tobaccos is provided, in the belief that Southern Rhodesia may be able thereby to cater effectively to Canada's requirements in tobaccos of the oriental type, hitherto imported entirely from non-empire countries.
The preference in favour of Australia on raisins and dried currants, which lapsed on March 31, last, is renewed, at four cents per pound.
An interesting and much anticipated item is that giving statutory recognition to the undertaking in connection with the United States under the recent agreement, relative to the privilege to be accorded to Canadians returning from abroad of bringing into Canada, free of duty, personal purchases to a value of $100.
Solely on the grounds of public health, the importation of textile waste derived from used mattresses is prohibited, unless such mattress waste be certificated as to proper fumigation, cleaning, etcetera.
In introducing the budget of May 1, 1930, I made the following statement regarding countervailing duties:
There are certain commodities which are or will become of double significance in Canada's trade with the world, both as imports and exports. On such commodities our policy has been, and is, to avoid extreme rates of duty, and we propose, regarding these products, to maintain in general the existing rates of duty.
It has been decided, however, to embody within the wording of a limited number of items of this class provision for a "countervailing duty" whereby Canada, while not generally raising its schedule rates, imposes upon such products from another country rates equivalent to those imposed by that country upon the identical Canadian product, where these are higher than the rates enumerated in the Canadian tariff schedule. This means that other countries who both buy from and sell to us these commodities, have it in their own power, by reciprocal action on their part, to enable us to reduce duties to the level of the rates stated in our tariff.
I have quoted my remarks of that date for the reason that they still serve perfectly to express my opinions regarding countervailing provisions which to-day's resolutions apply to three natural products: cut flowers, potatoes and eggs.
What about cast iron pipe?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
These three commodities were included in the list of May 1. 1930, and that they are again singled out for such treatment is due to the fact that the late administration in wiping out in September, 1930, the countervailing provisions of the May budget, did not provide, under the intermediate tariff, a duty more in line with the general tariff on eggs and, what is more important, failed to provide any duty whatsoever on potatoes or cut flowers. The weakness of Canada's bargaining position in respect of these commodities became speedily apparent in the Washington negotiations, so much so that this government declined to bind these items at the existing intermediate rate, thus giving clear indication that it might, at the first opportunity, see fit to recommend to parliament a revision of these ratings. In so recommending to-day, may I make clear that our attitude continues to be that of 1930; we do not desire or intend to raise tariffs; we do by the countervailing duties invite other countries to bring their tariffs down to the level of ours.
In 1935 there was inserted in the tariff item relating to steel plate a proviso to the effect that, regardless of any other law to the contrary, the anti-dumping provisions should not apply to plate more than 66 inches in width. Thus to select a solitary commodity for such treatment was, to say the least, to make an invidious distinction and it is proposed to allow the anti-dumping provision to apply to all products to which the law says it should, under given conditions, apply. In the interests of justice and equity, therefore, and without any regard whatsoever to the effect upon the quantum of tariff protection afforded, it is proposed to delete from this item the proviso in question.
There will be tabled to-day, in addition to those to which I have made specific reference, reports by the tariff board resulting from inquiries regarding the following commodities: Thrown yarns of artificial silk, buttons and button moulds, forged steel rolls, rice for processing, rhinestones and metal beads, containers of paperboard or fibreboard and photographic apparatus. Not all of these suggest or recommend tariff changes but, in accordance with the provisions of the Tariff Board Act, they will be made available to this house.
Regarding to-day's tariff proposals, may I say that these are formulated on the principle that the most enduring kind of progress is orderly progress-and that applies equally whether one's intended direction in the im-

The Budget-Mr. Dunning
position of taxes be downward or upward. Extremes defeat their own purpose; violent fluctuations one way or the other are mere leaps in the dark. Intelligent and unprejudiced appraisal of to-day's tariff situation in Canada will reveal sound reasons, apart altogether from the general principles 1 have just enunciated, why the best results are to be secured by deliberate, considered and related stages. There is, for example, our position with respect to British countries, to which I have referred. And, in the purely domestic sphere, there is the fact so readily overlooked: that this government, in extending to the United States the benefits of the intermediate tariff, effected at one stroke the most thorough-going downward revision of the customs tariff of Canada since the inception of that tariff-as a consequence of which act, together with the changes now proposed, commodities imported from the United States under at least 200 of the most important items in the tariff will pay lower rates of duty than they would have paid had they been so imported after the adoption of the May 1st budget of 1930.
In concluding this address, it is natural that my thoughts should go back to the last occasion on which I had the honour of presenting the budget six years ago to-day. The great change both in world conditions and conditions in Canada during that interval constitutes a challenge without precedent to the ability, the judgment and the broad patriotism of those charged with public responsibilities.
The government of Canada is making earnest and sustained efforts to meet this challenge and to grapple with the manifold problems of the country. I would ask the house and the country to accept the proposals I have made to-day as part of a conscientious effort to promote the best interests of the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has
grown up in this country a custom of not proceeding with the budget debate promptly on the conclusion of the address by the Finance minister. In the early days of the history of the dominion the debate was immediately proceeded with, but in view of the fact that a large portion of the budget speech, notably that comprising all the tariff changes, has not been read but has been placed on Hansard, where we shall have to read it in order to become familiar with the material contained in the tables and the details of the resolutions, it is obvious that the debate could not usefully be proceeded with now. I had intended, had the changes not been so extensive, to proceed at once, but from the very nature of the circumstances I shall be compelled to move now the adjournment of the debate. I do not know when it would be most convenient to resume it, but whatever suits the convenience of the government will be satisfactory to me.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As to proceeding with the debate on the budget, the government thought of proceeding on Monday, but if it would better suit the convenience of my right hon. friend we will make it Tuesday.

I greatly appreciate the
courtesy of the right hon. gentleman. I think the budget speech last year was delivered on a Thursday and we continued the debate on the following Tuesday, but it is quite immaterial whether this debate is resumed on Tuesday or Monday. If Tuesday is quite as satisfactory to the government we can make it Tuesday, but if the government prefers to go on with it on Monday we can proceed with it on Monday.

Other projects-to provide for the construction, repair and replacement of aids to navigation and buildings and structures used in connection therewith, $379,875.

us some details of this vote?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Marine):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This refers to a large number of items, chiefly repairs to lighthouses and work of that sort, which have been deferred for a number of years due to measures of economy. They do not appear in the main estimates of this year for the same reason, but in view of the fact that the work would be about seventy-five per cent labour, which would be distributed among a class of people who are very badly in need of help, namely the fishermen and those people living along our sea-coasts and inland waters, it was thought that this would be an opportune time to do this necessary work.
There is some provision for new construction; has the minister any information with regard to that?
Will any of this money be spent on inland waters?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.
How much?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I will give the figures for the different provinces. In Nova Scotia the amount to be expended totals $99,000; the total for the Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island agency is $11,800; for the New Brunswick agency, $31,625. The amount for the Quebec agency totals $17,500, which will cover work along the lower St. Lawrence river, while the $24,000 allotted to the Montreal agency will cover work on the upper St. Lawrence. The amount allotted to the Ontario agency is $53,500, which will cover work on lake Ontario and lake Erie.

Supply-Marine
Mr. CLARKE Rosedale): Will it go no further than lake Erie?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It will extend up to lake Superior. All the lakes are under the Ontario agency. The amount allotted to the British Columbia agency is $32,450.
Are any repairs being done this year to the piers at Hamilton beach? The minister may not be able to furnish this information immediately and perhaps he can give it to me later on.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: This vote does not cover canals, which would come under the Department of Railways and Canals. This is a Department of Marine vote.

Is any provision being made to furnish greater protection to boats between the mouth of the Red river and the pleasure resorts at the south of lake Winnipeg? The lake at that point is treacherous and a number of lives have been lost. Representations have been made to me by the board of trade of Winnipeg and others asking that the small expenditure necessary be made by the department to make this end of the lake a great deal safer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Two or three lights are to be built at Winnipeg Beach under this vote. My officials believe that these will give the required aids to navigation on lake Winnipeg.
Would it be possible to have some sort of telephone service or signals to give warning of approaching storms?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The matter of signals has been considered by the lighthouse board, but that board has not recommended them and they are not included. I may say that this lighthouse board is made up of the senior officials of the Department of Marine and others. It passes on all applications for lights, signals or anything in the way of aids to navigation, and ordinarily unless the application passes the board no appropriation is made.

Does this item provide for the maintenance of navigation signals? I have reference to the difficulties that arose recently in connection with needed repairs to navigation signals in the port of Vancouver. These signals went out of operation recently and one of the West Vancouver ferries ran aground. It took several days to secure the services of an expert from Victoria. I should like to know if provisions are being made whereby these signals may be quickly repaired should they go out of order, particularly during the foggy season.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I may say that the repairs mentioned by my hon. friend have been made already. This vote includes $15,000 for rebuilding Burnaby shoals beacon.
Will there also be available expert repair men for immediate repairs of any breakdowns in the signals?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Arrangements have been
made with the Vancouver harbour commissioners that any repairs required to the lights, even though they are not within the jurisdiction of the harbour, will in future be attended to by the mechanics of the Vancouver harbour commission. We think that will be quite an improvement.
Will any proportion of this amount be spent in Toronto harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
There is no amount in this
item for Toronto harbour.

The amount allowed to
British Columbia, I understood, was $32,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext:
One item alone has $15,000
earmarked for it. That does not leave very much for the numerous aids required in the district I represent and that of Skeena. It is evident that the minister has not allowed -at least I ask him if he has considered- the removal of Ripple rock in Seymour narrows? That would cost a lot of money, I admit, but it is a necessary undertaking. Some day, if the matter is not attended to, it is going to cost an enormous loss of life. The rock is submerged about ten feet at low tide. A heavy current runs through there; there is a side current which comes in from a side channel and which tends to drift boats over on to this rock; and all boats of any size, unless they are very powerful, have to wait perhaps five or six hours in order to fit the tide, because they can go in only on slack water, which is a very short time. Some years ago an American boat went up there, struck a rock and pierced her bottom. Lucidly they happened to be able to beach her without loss of life. But traffic there is increasing all the time; there are more boats, and the pressure of keeping up schedules compels them to take a greater chance. Some day a most disastrous marine accident is going to occur there. I have not taken this up with the present minister, but in years gone by I have repeatedly put it up to past governments, and they have all promised consideration. I admit that a large sum would be required. I believe that at one time shipping interests were so much
Supply-M arine

concerned that the United States government made a suggestion that they share part of the expense of the work, because their traffic used the Seymour narrows so much and the danger was so great. But the Canadian government of that time did not think it would be dignified to accept such an offer, or there was some other reason. But if the department is spending money now in a large way for work of that kind I suggest that, if it is not too late, the minister might at least consider that project. I am sure that he will have records with full information on file in his office.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The item in question was
carefully considered but it was left out for two reasons. One is because it would cost somewhere between $300,000 and $500,000, and the second is that it is work which requires very little labour. In this particular schedule we have taken only items where not less than fifty per cent of the expenditure is labour. The purpose of this estimate is to furnish some help to the people along the shore who have been having a bad time. But I shall be glad to look into the matter further and perhaps at some future time under another program we shall be able to do the work. My officers realize that it is quite necessary.

I thank the minister for
his promise. I admit that a great deal of labour would not be involved, but I think his information regarding the cost is inaccurate. I believe it could be done for $150,000. We had, I think estimates of that cost. I know there are engineers' estimates in the department; whatever their amount is would no doubt be correct. I am speaking only from memory of some years ago, but I thought it did not exceed $150,000.
Mr. MacNEI'L:	Has provision been made
n this item for the repair of floats at the smaller settlements along the coast to enable steamships to call?

Item agreed to.
To provide for the reconditioning and conversion of government steamers, $175,000.
Does this cover any provision for replacing the boat called the Newington, on the Pacific coast? It is a lighthouse tender.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, it does. This is a
constructive item, and it is one that I have sponsored personally. We find that we have in the Department of Marine a great number of boats, many of which are over
[Mr. Neill.)
twenty years old and in bad condition. The objection that I found to this work of the department was that all these boats were for special purposes, and after they had performed their little service they were through for the season. The purpose of this item is to revamp several boats and allow them to serve a double purpose. Each boat that is revamped will serve its present purpose and one other. We have now at Sorel a suitable boat which we are going to recondition to replace the Newington. We intend to put in a double bottom, make it into a first-class boat and send it to Prince Rupert. It has ample power and cruising range, and with a few alterations will be very suitable to take the place of the Newington.

That is gratifying, because
this has been a long-felt want; the service is requiring more boats all the time. When may we expect to have that boat on the Pacific?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We hope to finish the alterations this summer. I should think it will be round there this fall, in September or October.
Which boat is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is coal barge No. 7.

I suggest that it be given
a proper name, appropriate to the west coast where it is going to operate. It might be called the Alberni instead of being designated by a number.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I shall be glad to consider
that.

Beyond that, what are
the particulars of the $175,000? Has the minister the particulars?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes. It is intended to take
the ice-breaker Saurel, do away with its palatial passenger accommodation and make it into a buoy boat as well as an ice-breaker. As we know, it has tremendous power. With a few alterations and some additional equipment it will be able to handle buoys and it will take the place of the Druid, which is a very old boat, and expensive to operate.

What is it estimated
that it will cost?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That cost is $50,000. Then
there is provision for the refitting of the Dollard. The Dollard is a buoy boat operating out of Saint John. By revamping the boilers and giving it greater cruising range it will do its own work and also the work now handled by the Laoirentian, a second buoy boat. We have mentioned coal barge No. 7,

Supply-Marine
which will replace the Newington. We have in Quebec a tug called the Citadelle, which is fitted up as a fire tug. It has never thrown a stream of water. It is a very powerful tug. One of its purposes was to turn the Empress of Britain, but private tugs have come into Quebec to do the work to the satisfaction of the Canadian Pacific; they say that they have no further use for the Citadelle. We will have a separate fire tug which will do the work as well as the Citadelle. We propose to refit the accommodation so that it can replace the Jalobert, now used as the pilot boat at Father Point. It is adequate for that service, and in winter months after its bow has been strengthened, it can be used on the Nova Scotia coast for ice-breaking in the harbours there. It is a lighter boat than the one now in use; I am told that it will foe quite adequate for this work, and that a considerable saving will be made.
What was the amount again?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext: Is it the intention of the minister to abandon the Laurentian?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, after we have been satisfied that the Dollard can do the service adequately we intend to lay up the Laurentian.

The changes mentioned by the minister are changes that we considered many months ago, I do not say in detail, but in the broad principle. While I am not an expert, from the evidence that was presented to me I was of opinion in connection with these old steamers, anywhere from ten to twenty or twenty-five years old-
I think that is the oldest-that to undertake to rebuild a boat constructed for a special purpose, and to reboiler her, having regard to changed conditions in regard to the production of steam and the utilization of other mechanical devices for the production of motive power, was a doubtful venture. For instance, modern science has made great improvements in even the last ten years. In connection with boats for the purpose of taking up and putting down buoys, for example, we have had tremendous changes since the first boat was built for that purpose.
I noticed that the last boat I saw, built for that class of work, was of entirely different construction from the one I saw many years before. The question of marine equipment, such as cranes, and the rapidity with which power can be applied to windlasses and cap-12739-155
stans for the purpose of moving a boat, and that sort of thing, made me douibt whether it was sound economy, apart from anything else, to attempt to recondition these boats. The minister says that he has satisfied himself on the point, and obviously his training has been more closely allied to matters of this kind than mine, but I certainly doubt whether it is sound economy to undertake what he says is being done. Certainly these boats cannot work in the winter if they are equipped only for lifting and putting down the buoys in the St. Lawrence, because the buoys are taken up in the fall and put down in the spring, and a special boat for that purpose cannot be utilized in the winter time for general purposes in Nova Scotia or anywhere else. In other places, where there are continuously sounding buoys, spar buoys and matters of that kind constantly in place, it is the duty of these boats to see that such buoys do not move out of place so that they become faulty aids to navigation. If the minister has satisfied himself, obviously I can only point out to him that the effort we made to see how some of these steamers might be repaired at not too great a cost induced me to believe that for the purposes the minister has suggested it would be sound economy to build new boats. That is all I desire to say in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We are fortunate, I think, in having in the Department of Marine, in charge at Sorelj, Mr. David Carswell, who was appointed by the late government. He is an able shipbuilder; I know him very well and I have great confidence in him. I might point out to my right hon. friend that the boats we are proposing to remodel are our newest boats. For instance, the Saurel is a splendid ice-breaker, but once it is through breaking ice we have no use for it unless, perhaps, it may be used to carry the governor general.
It took him to the Magdalen islands.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes. It is a splendid boat, and it is a pity that it can work only for a month in the spring, breaking ice, and for a month in the fall, keeping the channel open.
The N. B. McLean is in the same class, except that it is sent to Hudson bay.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes. The Saurel is our second best ice-breaker and we feel that if we can keep it in service during the summer, if it will do the work of another boat, it is good economy to spend $50,000 on it for equip-

Supply-Marine

ment. I may say that the Citadelle is practically the newest boat we have; it is almost a brand new tug, and its earnings last year were S600. As far as a fire tug goes, a much smaller boat with less power is equally useful, because it must have steam up twenty-four hours a day. Otherwise its only duty is to pump water in case of fire, so in replacing that boat we are releasing a splendid ship which we can use pretty well the year round as a combination pilot boat and ice-breaker, for the small amount of ice-breaking required along the Nova Scotia coast. We feel thatin this way we can keep that boat occupied twelve months a year.

I think I should say to the minister that I do not believe it is sound economy to eliminate entirely the maintenance of a boat for fire protection in Quebec, as long as we have the present type of ships coming there and tying up to the docks and the number of passengers who are landed there. My inquiries, both on this and on the other side of the water, satisfied me that although it might look expensive, nevertheless the maintenance of a fire boat seemed almost essential. The minister knows the great discussion that has taken place over the question of a fire boat at Quebec. The Citadelle, as he says, was not intended originally as a fire boat, but she was provided with equipment which enables her to throw a stream of water well over the sheds at Wolfe's cove, according to my memory, though I speak subject to correction. Only a few months ago I was discussing the matter of fire boat protection in these harbours, and it appears to be the universal opinion that you must have it. In New York, as the minister probably knows better than I do a great deal of money has been thus used; this is one of the matters to which they have paid great attention, and I think it has a profound effect, if I might use that word, upon the whole question of insurance as dealt with by Lloyd's and other world underwriters. I merely mention this because, when we came into office and during succeeding years, discussions regarding a fire boat at Quebec were numerous. Ultimately this boat was equipped for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I should like to make it quite clear that we are not taking away from Quebec anything in the way of fire protection. We are sending there a boat not nearly as heavily engined as the Citadelle but we are transferring all the fine pumps and monitors from the Citadelle to this smaller boat.
Will she carry them?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, she is quite capable of carrying them, and this will have the effect of releasing the Citadelle for other work.

With regard to the suggestion of the leader of the opposition concerning the advisability of continuing steam power on these boats, I think it is a fair statement to say that older engineers in this country are partial to steam, from long acquaintance, and that the advent of Diesel power perhaps is not received as favourably as it would be by younger men. Whether these boats should be refitted with steam power is a matter for the technical department. I am glad of one thing, however, that we shall have more ice-breaking facilities on the coast of Nova Scotia, because many times during last winter we found that neither the Marine department nor the Fisheries department had a boat available to do the work along our coast.
There is another suggestion that I might make. The coast of Nova Scotia extends for quite a distance, and Halifax is sixteen miles in from the sea. One or more of these boats could very well make their headquarters in some other port and so be closer to the scene of operations when called on. The fact that the Marine department has headquarters in Halifax is no reason why the boats should all be quartered there, and when a boat is called for at Yarmouth or Sydney it should not have to go all that distance. If the boats were stationed along the coast one would always be closer and more available when needed.
Would Saint John satisfy you?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The Montcalm which is stationed in Nova Scotia waters makes her headquarters at Sydney. This year we found it impossible to do with the Montcalm all the work we were called upon to do. Our idea in having the Citadelle available was that it could work in the southern part of the province and so avoid the necessity of the Montcalm cruising such great distances. We were unable to give satisfaction, and it probably has been a very expensive year for operations.
You will have to change the bows of the Citadelle.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes, we are remodelling and strengthening it as part of the repairs.

To provide for the removal of derelicts in the harbours of Canada, particularly Port Arthur, Fort William, Sarnia, South Bay and Richelieu river, $70,000.

Before the minister speaks on this item, perhaps I should point out that all these three items properly belong to the main estimates, and ordinarily would be found there. He has anticipated placing them in the main or general estimates, and is placing them in these special supplementaries for the reason he has given. These harbours are-I was going to say periodically-raked for derelicts and I thought were fairly clear at the present time, in view of the efforts made in that direction during the last few years. I mean not the last two, but the last few years, because in connection with operations at Port Arthur and Fort William, for instance, the firm which had in hand the placing of that new breakwater and the performance of certain dredging operations cleared out from the harbour-I would not describe them so much as derelicts but impediments to uniform depth of water in both harbours. The minister knows that dredging operations were carried on there in more recent years for the purpose of providing uniform depth of water in both harbours, and of ensuring safety of navigation. My information was that the harbour was swept fairly clear of these derelicts.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Ordinarily we have in the
main estimates an item for the removal of obstructions. This year the item was cut down to take care only of the work under way. We had one or two wrecks on which work was progressing and provided simply for it, the removal of obstructions being a thing we could defer, and we were pruning these estimates as much as we could. However, the removal of derelicts provides a large percentage of labour-
Does it? I thought not; I thought machines and a very small amount of labour were used.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
We had a report made on
*these particular derelicts and we found the work of removal was about sixty per cent direct and indirect labour, which brought it into the class of work we were looking for. We are constantly having applications for this work. We have recently made stricter the regulations preventing the beaching of derelicts; it is the duty of every harbour master and other officials to report immediately such beaching to Ottawa when legal action is considered. We hope to prevent these practices in the future. But we have a great number of these. In Port Arthur I think there were some fifteen.

Are they beached or
under water?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Partly beached and partly
under water. The underwater ones are cleaned out in the main channels. In Sarnia-

There were two in the
channel there at one time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes; it seems to have been
the practice in the past, if you got tired of your boat, simply to take it to Port Arthur or Fort William or Sarnia and leave it.

I thought it "left" the
crew.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, possibly. In any event
we have this great number of derelicts. Pressure has been brought to bear upon the department for many years to take care of them, and we felt that this was a proper time.

The minister says that
pressure has been brought to bear upon the department for many years. I may say that ever since I have known anything of the government there has never been a time when there were not some derelicts removed. All the derelicts were not in sea channels, either.
The particular matter I desired to draw attention to is the Richelieu river. I observe that the minister has had his attention directed to it. It has been suggested that an effort is to be made to open a channel to the United States by utilizing the Richelieu river and certain canals. Has this work anything to do with that possibility? That is the only other question I desired to ask about this item.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The item at first covered
Fort William, Port Arthur, Sarnia and South Bay. It was enlarged at the last minute to take care of the Richelieu river.
I can readily understand its being enlarged.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I have not the exact details but we have a small item here for work in the Richelieu river.

But has it to do with
that transcendently important matter of reaching the Atlantic through the Richelieu river and canals down into the state of New York? Recently there has been considerable discussion in United States papers, less in Canadian papers, looking to that ultimate design behind such a work, and I wanted to know from the minister whether or not the suggestion of clearing the channel of the Richelieu river had anything to do with the projected work. The minister knows to what I refer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Yes, quite.
2426	COMMONS
Supply-Marine-National Harbours Board

It has in view using the river and canals for the purpose of reaching the Atlantic ocean without going out past Quebec at all. by a certain type of small tonnage vessel and by barges. I think there was a time when this route was quite extensively used for barges of small size, but that was long ago. This suggestion I think was in part put forward by certain engineers in New York and apparently certain Canadian engineers thought well of it. I was interested to know whether or not this item contemplates any expenditure for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This will do useful and, I
think, necessary work preliminary to that, in cleaning out the channel. The international waterways commission are studying the particular question to which my right bon. friend refers, and we were asked to delegate an engineer to work with them on the project. This is merely cleaning up the river; however, the work will be useful if anything develops the other way.

I call the attention of
the minister to the fact that this item refers mostly to western harbours. In. Sydney harbour we have a derelict which the former government tried unsuccessfully to raise and which is still left with us. I think about $2,600 was expended on the raising of that derelict, but still she lies there, a menace to navigation and an eyesore to the people as well as to incoming passengers. I should like to hear from the minister that action will be taken to remove that old derelict.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I should like to say that
there is a contract for the removal of the Pelican, and there is an item in the other estimates to pay for the cost of that work. We are having some difficulty, but we are hopeful that sufficient funds will be made available to complete the removal of that wreck.

At the time these items were decided upon did the minister have before him an application for the removal of a number of derelicts from the harbour of Kingston? I know that in the past representations were made to the Department of Public Works for the removal of those boats, and some information was obtained about them. Over a period of years representations have been made, quite a number of those derelicts would be standing in the Rideau river; they are just inside the causeway. Have those derelicts been considered by the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
I was not aware of any
applications, but my deputy advises me that
IMr. Howe.]
some time ago representations were made. No fresh representations have been made since I took over the department. So far as I recall, the removal of those derelicts is not included in the item.

Item agreed to.
National Harbours Board-Projects already undertaken-Halifax harbour improvements- to provide for payment of amounts retained in connection with certain contracts, four at $500 each, $2,000.
Mr, BENNETT:	What does this item
refer to, and why should it be in the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It is to provide for amounts
retained on certain contracts.

Why should we have to
come to parliament to get power to return the money? I realize the amount is small.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: It is the intention in connection with harbours that for this fiscal year all amounts expended will be voted by parliament. We are doing away with blanket amounts.

Oh, yes, but the power
to return money put up in connection with contracts has never required a vote of parliament, so far as I am aware. I was j-ust asking why the minister comes to parliament to get power to return a man his own money that had been put up in connection with a contract. Either he is entitled to it, in which case no legislation is required, or if he is not entitled to it obviously we should not give it to him without knowing why it is being given.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Nevertheless we must provide for it, and we have no fund for the purpose, other than what is voted by parliament.

This is money that has
been put up.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: No.

The item refers to
"amounts retained- in connection with certain contracts."

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

It is the contractor's
money, not ours.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
As my right hon. friend
knows, progress estimates are voted less ten per cent. Ninety per cent is paid and ten per cent is held back. The work has been practically completed, and the hold backs have been reduced to $2,000. Nevertheless

Supply-Marine-Saint John Harbour
we have no funds available to pay that $2,000. We are not holding contractors' money; it is money deducted from progress estimates.

I follow the minister.
The explanation is that inasmuch as the harbour had no funds, this sum is merely to pay the balance of a contract price, and is not to return any drawback?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is correct.
It is the balance of a contract price.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

Item agreed to.
Saint J ohn harbour improvements-reconstruction of berths, 1, 2, 3 and 4, $1,817,506.
Would the minister give us an explanation of how this matter now stands. The contract was let in our time What is the position to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We are continuing the contract, but at the present time we are having considerable difficulty. I do not know that the points at issue are public property, but there has been a considerable slide of material on the face of that property.

And always will be.
Mr.	HOWE: So	much so	that the	contractor has stopped	work and	has demanded
a readjustment of his contract.
Mr.	BENNETT:	Is that	quite the	fair
way to put it? Was it not that the department instructed certain things to be done and in consequence of their being done the ultimate result was that he declined to continue. They would not let him do it the way the specifications provided.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No, I think my right hon. friend	is mistaken.	I have	followed	the
matter closely, because it is a condition which has given us a great deal of alarm. It is true that some instructions were given that cylinders were to be sunk ahead of the piles, but it is a purely local matter which affects only some ten per cent of the length of the work. The contractor is at liberty to construct the rest of it any way he wishes to do so, but he does not care to proceed with the work unless a readjustment is made.
Was he not interfered with?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No, that is not my information, I may say that I made a special trip to Saint John. The contractor claimed that he had been interfered with. I made it clear
at the time that the order in which work would be done would be left definitely to the contractor, and it has been since that time.
But prior to that time a definite order was given as to the way in which work was to be done, was there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think it is open to question as to whether the instructions given could be construed as an order. I think if the contractor had not cared to make an issue of it the matter would have been straightened out. However I think we have made the situation clear. As I see it there is no reflection upon the contractor; it is a situation which has arisen, but which was not expected by our officers. It is giving us a great deal of concern, and we hope to straighten it out over a period of time. I am simply reporting at this time that the matter is very much in a state of flux.

This is a matter in which I have something more than ordinary personal interest. I was bom not far from there, and when these berths were burned the question as to how they should be replaced became a matter of great interest. We sought the opinion of our departmental engineers, and they wanted cribwork berths. After the soundings were taken it seemed to be clear that to reach hard pan they would have to go down as far as seventy or eighty, and in one case over eighty feet, which is a tremendous distance. The bank is of mud, bay of Fundy mud, and it slopes sharply into the harbour. I remember that when we came into office we had on our hands the construction of west Saint John works; the coffer dam went out twice, and it cost us for extras something like one and a half times the original contractors' bid for the construction of the work, which made me very, very anxious about this particular undertaking. Without being an expert I favoured, personally, a cylindrical concrete pile for the purpose of preventing what I regarded as lateral pressure on the structure forcing it into the harbour. The lack of stability that would come about from the construction of a wooden pile berth would not have been satisfactory; the mooring of a heavy ship would undoubtedly have had a bad effect. I have been around the berths at which heavy ships have been moored, and could almost feel the berths moving. Some of our engineers, probably all of them, did not think it was desirable to put in pile work. The matter was referred to two consulting engineers, one of whom was the chief engineer of the Canadian Pacific railway, who gave us his advice,
2428	COMMONS
Supply-Marine-Saint John Harbour
and the other was the most eminent consulting engineer available in the city of Montreal. I believe his name was Mr. James; that is my recollection. He concurred in the view that the cylindrical concrete pile would be advisable.
The contract was let on the basis of concrete cylindrical piles. My information from inquiry the other day as to how the work was progressing indicated that there had been, shall I say interference from the department with the work as being carried on by the contractors. My inquiry was not from the contractors but from another source. The information was that the contractors had been told that they were to do the work in a certain way which, having regard to the terms of the plans and specifications they thought was undesirable, because it is a tremendous task first of all to prepare the hole, and, second, to build up the cylindrical foundations at a depth of seventy-five or eighty feet in the mud of the bay of Fundy, where it is sharply slipping into the river. It is a tremendous task, and the plans and specifications contemplated some of the difficulties as to the manner in which the work should be carried on. I was informed'-and this is the reason I asked the question-that there was some interference from the department here with the contractors, the net result being that they .said: This is not the way in which we contracted to do this work, and if we are to be subjected to these directions we must have a clear understanding before we go further. It must be. remembered that some of the cylinders are being cast; some have been cast. The cylinders, as the minister knows as an engineer-and I need hardly mention it-are not cast in place but are cast on the ground and put into their place on the sinking of the holes-you might really call them shafts because they are from seventy-five to eighty feet in depth-and that is a matter of some difficulty, though, I understand, not of any great difficulty from an engineering standpoint. But they are always subjected to pressure. The lateral pressure that Sir Alexander Gibb referred to in connection with the dock at Wolfe's Cove was so apparent that this great property was really moving towards the river. At first the movement was not very great, but he recommended that we should take immediate action to prevent that lateral pressure from moving the great structure further into the river, and it has cost substantial sums of money to take the necessary steps to prevent that lateral pressure making itself effective. I am more interested in these new berths at Saint John than in many of these matters because of its location and my

desire to see berths built there in keeping with the work at west Saint John which was finished only a few short months ago, and in keeping with pier B in Halifax harbour. The conditions at Saint John are very difficult. The people of Saint John themselves carried on the necessary undertakings for a number of years, and now that the harbour is in the hands of the commission it is of the utmost importance that this work should be finished as contemplated.
The minister says that there was no suggestion that resulted in action being delayed. But finally the contractors said that if somer body else was to determine how they should do their work they would leave it to that somebody else rather than undertake it themselves. That is a short way of putting the situation, and I wanted information on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: First of all, I do not like to say at this time whether the design adopted was the best or not, because I never had imuch use for engineers who would come in after trouble developed and say that they would have done the work in some other way; so we will leave that out of the question.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
My attention was first
brought to the situation at Saint John in January when I had a call from the contractor. He said that he was somewhat in doubt about the work there, and he referred to certain instructions. They were issued not from Ottawa but from the harbour commission; it was before there was any attempt at centralization. He asked me to go down and look at the work personally, and I did so. I went down with the general manager for the contractor and I made it clear at that time, and have done so since, because I have had a great deal of experience in handling contracts, that it is the contractor's privilege bo handle his work in any way he likes provided the work in the end is done according to the plans and specifications. I made it clear that that was his privilege, and he was quite satisfied at the time that he had a free hand to do his work in his own way so long as he produced the proper results. The developments were as much a surprise to the contractor as they were to us, perhaps not exactly a surprise because when- you look back at what happened you might reason that it might have been expected. However, trouble has developed and we are doing our best to overcome it. I do not want to repeat the experience of the past and let the cost run

Supply-Marine-Saint John Harbour
away so that eventually it is twice the sum contemplated. We are working very hard in the department to permit the work to be done as originally planned without increasing the cost to the government, and in the course of another week I have the hope that we shall see daylight.

How much has been
spent already?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: To the end of March, $823,539.

Is this the balance of
the contract or the whole sum?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The whole sum required.
So it should be something like $800,000 less than we are really voting because $800,000 has already been spent.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
These are requirements in
addition to the $823,539. The sum of $2,000,000 was voted under the Public Works Contract Act, 1934, and the contract price was $2,641,039.

The leader of the opposition
has asked a question I was going to ask. Is this additional for the amount of the contract, and for unforeseen expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
It is the balance required
to finish the contract that has been placed. The amount appropriated under the Public Works Construction Act, 1934, was less than the contract price, and this is the amount required to complete the contract.
Which added to the sum already paid, will complete the contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Correct.

As this item comes under
the supplementary estimates dealing more or less with relief, I would ask the minister to see that the contractors engage local labour as much as possible. I was pleased to hear the leader of the opposition state that he was anxious to have this work completed, but we in the city of Saint John would have been much better satisfied if he had expressed the same anxiety two or three years ago, because the delay in starting this work has been a great handicap to the port of Saint John. Some years ago the house voted unanimously for the carrying out of this work, but for a reason which could probably be explained by the leader of the opposition himself this undertaking was delayed for two or three years.

Not for two or three
years.
A couple of years anyway.
Not a couple.
And pressure was brought to bear upon the then government to go on with that work.

That is not so, but it
does not make any difference.

Living in Saint John I am
familiar with what has taken place there.
But not here.

And had the leader of the
opposition expressed the same anxiety a couple of years ago that he does to-day we would now be much better off in the port of Saint John.

That is about the thanks one would expect from the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Ryan) for the interest that one has in the harbour there. After the fire there would not have been a berth there at all of the class now being built but for the interest we took in it. Great difficulties were experienced in west Saint John, and the cost of those facilities was tremendous, beyond all reason. The contract had been let before the late government came into office, and the works were not finished there until the end of 1934. Two coffer dams went out in the meantime, and the extras that we had to pay under a contract that never should have been made were 150 per cent more than the original contract itself. We paid $600,000 in settlement for extras on a contract foT $400,000 because coffer dams went out on two occasions.
When this matter came up we realized that it was not local but national. It is a national port and it affects the whole of Canada. The west is as deeply interested in it as is Saint John, and we determined to try and get berths there that at least would not slip into the harbour and that would not bring about the difficulties which had been experienced with the other west Saint John works. Four engineers from the departments of Railways and Canals, Marine, Public Works and National Defence went down there at my personal insistence and investigated the matter. They took the greatest possible care in preparing their recommendations. I have said that they were of the opinion that cribwork would be better, first, because it was less expensive in times of economic difficulty and, second, because they believed that having regard to the situation and the conditions prevailing, it would be desirable to have that
2430	COMMONS
Supply-Marine-Chicoutimi Harbour
type of berth. Perhaps it was a case where fools rush in where angels fear to tread. I had a strong personal opinion that it was desirable that these berths should be built upon concrete cylindrical piers and I arrived at that conclusion because of certain investigations I had made on one occasion into a harbour in Great Britain. It later developed that the borers had made their appearance in that harbour, but that was after the contract had been let. I am not quite sure as to the time, but I think it was after the contract had been let. At any rate, we referred the matter to a consulting engineer; we referred it to the Canadian Pacific engineer and finally with the aid of Mr. Gray, the resident engineer, who was in favour of concrete cylindrical piers, we had plans and specifications prepared and asked for tenders. We were told that there were very few contractors in this country who could do this work.
We are now told that if we had been as much interested in this two years ago the situation would have been a good deal better than it is now. It is because we were so much interested in it that we succeeded in having the contract let for the construction of these berths with concrete cylinders. This was in accordance with the views held by tihe resident engineer and in keeping with one of the best berth facilities provided in the old country in one of its harbours. I have the interest which a native son is always permitted to have in the development of the harbour of Saint John, not only because it happens to be in New Brunswick but because it is one of the national harbours on the Atlantic coast upon which the west and other par,ts of Canada must rely to reach the sea and the markets of the world during the winter season. The effort that has been made has been continuous. It involved a lot of money and I want to say that the efforts to get that money were at times very great. At the expense of other works which were delayed we went forward with this although the very limited number of men who were prepared to tender on the work made it more difficult than it otherwise would have been. We are now told that if we had been a little more anxious about it, it would have been a little better for Saint John. This is a very good illustration of the ingratitude which follows public life.

Item agreed to.
Chicoutimi harbour improvements-road to make connection between dock and new bridge and connecting dock sidings with Roberval and Saguenay terminal, $13,663.52.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
This item is to complete
item 28 of the Public Works Construction

Act, 1934. It is a small amount to finish up a contract already let.

Has the minister visited
this harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Unfortunately I have not.

I was hoping he had as
I should like to have his frank opinion as to whether or not the works at this place can ever be justified in their present location. We found them there as part of the, shall I say legacy that we had to take over. I am not complaining about that, but large commitments were made involving the expenditure of vast sums of money. Has the minister before him a statement of what has been spent there? I do not want to put him to any great trouble, but I should like to know what has been spent up to the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: If the right hon. gentleman will allow me to give that when we are discussing the harbour estimates, I shall be prepared with the full information.
That is quite satisfactory.

This brings up a point in connection with several of these items. The minister, I understand, has said that provision was made for this work in the Public Works Construction Act, 1935. I have always been of the opinion that it was not necessary to revote items which appeared in that act in the same manner as we revote items in the regular estimates. The items in the Public Works Construction Aot, 1934, were carried on without being revoted, and I am of opinion that it is not necessary to revote in this instance. Statutory appropriations are made available until the work is completed. I do not know just why these items appear in these estimates when provision has already been made. It may be the government's policy, but it seems to me that this is not necessary at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: As a matter of government policy we believe that it is better to budget for the items and have them show in the expenditures for this year, but I may say that some of the public works items have been curtailed and we believe that as of April 1 we should note the money we are spending this year.
Although it has once been voted?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: That is quite true, but I understand it is intended to repeal these acts.

The effect of this is really to pad the estimates; you are making it

Supply-Marine-Quebec Harbour
appear that you are providing for works that have already been provided for. At the end of the estimates is an analysis of the expenditures and the total for projects already undertaken is $30,418,341.66. I take it that funds for these items have already been provided for under the public works construction acts. As I say, the effect of this method is to create the impression that a large amount of money is being provided this year for works whereas the money was provided in years gone by.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I do not know that the money was provided, but the expenditures were authorized. I think the people who are spending the money this year will have to find it. We prefer to wipe out the former appropriations and appropriate the money again and we shall have to find the money to be expended on these works during this fiscal year.

Putting them into these estimates is not finding the money any more than it would be finding the money by putting them into the regular estimates. Did the minister say that it was the intention of the government to repeal the public works construction acts of 1934 and 1935?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I cannot announce that definitely, as that would be the privilege of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), but that is my understanding as we were asked to provide for work for the current year, whether or not it appeared in the public works construction acts of 1934 and 1935.
In any event, this Chicoutimi item would require an appropriation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes; I understand it is an addition.
That is different if it is in addition to what has been provided already.
Could the minister tell us if any part of the projects mentioned here are already completed and, if so, what is the total amount of those completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I may say that the Halifax project is all completed. That S2,000 is purely for hold back that is required until certain terms of the contracts have been complied with. In the case of Chicoutimi the expenditure last year was $153,500, and this $13,500 completes the work there.

Item agreed to.
Quebec harbour improvements-
To provide for payment of amounts retained in connection with certain contracts, $6,866.71.
New quay wall-To widen west side, pier No. 1, Princess Louise docks, $808,202.73.
Bituminous macadam road, Gilmour hill- provision for payment of claim for additional work done under contract, $7,177.92.
Dredging at Wolfe's Cove terminal, $179,906.70. Dredging St. Charles river and Louise basin, $203,355.81.
Resurfacing Wolfe's Cove yard, $18,159.53. Repairs to wharves and sheds, Princess Louise docks, $17,000.

I should like to ask two or three questions about that. First, how much of the total $1,240,000 has been spent? Second, are contracts outstanding for all the work there mentioned? Third, why is it necessary to revote money that was the subject matter of much discussion in this house and with respect to which there was no lapsing of the estimate? The point I desire to make to the minister is that the old estimate did not lapse at the end of the fiscal year. Why are we voting this a second time? I was on the other side when we were putting it through a year ago, endeavouring to explain why it had come about that we had to make the expenditure. Now I should like to know whether the contracts are let, how much has been expended, and why it is necessary to vote this a second time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The first item under this is a sum of $6,866 to provide for the clearing up of certain contracts. I think that is similar to the item for Halifax, that is retained percentages that will be released. Then there is the new quay wall for the Princess Louise docks, $808,202. That is a contract which was let some months ago to the Ogilvie Construction Company. There was some difficulty about engineering, and when we came into office we found it in a very unsatisfactory state, and decided, not to cancel the contract but to suspend the work until we could review the engineering. We have now reviewed the engineering and revised it. We are voting the amount of that contract here so that we can go on with the work this summer.
Is it a new contract, or do the old contractors carry it on?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We have made no rearrangement of the contract. They still have the contract although they have not done any work, and I assume we can readjust the matter with them so that they can carry it on.
When was the original contract drawn?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

speechtext:
In what way does the minister mean that he did not agree with the

Supply-Marine-Quebec Harbour
engineering? Were the plans submitted not satisfactory to the department and to the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: We found that the plans had been changed, I think, three times from the time the contract was let until the time that I reviewed the matter.
It was a question of the condition of the existing works, which had not been looked after for a long time, plus the question of widening the berth.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I think they were working on the third plan. The contract had been let on a plan that was not suitable for the location. When the nature of the bottom was found, changes were necessary, and changes were made. For some reason or another the second plan was not satisfactory, and at the time I was there the third plan was under consideration.

And yet the contract
had been let.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
The contract was let, yes.
These changes were made after the contract was let.
That was a contract by the harbour commission, was it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
No, it was under the Public
Works Construction Act.

I wonder whether the
minister could let us know if the amount in the present estimate was the original amount of the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: The amount of the contract is $734,000. The amount of $808,000 includes supervision. It is the same vote for that project as is in the Public Works Construction Act. We have revoted it as it was.
Is this not a correct way to put it: The plans and specifications were prepared by a consulting engineer, who loked after Three Rivers and two or three other harbours.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Mr. Gohier.

Yes. He has had considerable experience, according to my information, and he was regarded very highly in his profession, but I understand his politics were not quite satisfactory after the change of government.
Order.

Order! Yes, it was in
order that they were unsatisfactory. But what happened in consequence of that was

that difficulties were raised about the plans and specifications. The contract had actually been let, as I recollect, before the change of government took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
Three months before. But
the contract had been changed twice before this government came into power. The plans had been changed twice.

I was going to continue: The plans and specifications contemplated changes and alterations of the existing contract; on investigation it was found that the conditions of that existing work were much worse than were apparent at the time the contract was made, and the contractor immediately pointed that out. Is that not the fact? I think that will be found to be the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Yes.

I am not quite sure
about this, because I am carrying all these particulars in my head, and they cover every part of Canada. The minister knows perfectly well that with regard to the old harbour one of two things has to be done: Either we have to spend some money, or all the outcome of that vast expenditure there will ultimately crumble and fall away. I refer to the work on the King's wharf and to the Louise basin and the work at what is called the Old harbour. We had reports from time to time about that Old harbour, and it will be recalled that when the last appropriation was made to the harbour commissioners it was stated in this house, when that resolution was before it, that that would be the last money which would be asked for Quebec, because the sum spent there has been very large; my memory is that it is something like $50,000,000 for that harbour. When Wolfe's Cove was finally chosen as the site for this new wharf a shed was put there which would do credit to New York; it is a magnificent double-decked shed. The berth itself was inspected by Sir Alexander Gibb. He found that lateral pressure was gradually pushing it towards the river, and we took steps to remedy that. There remained one other question with respect to 'that. On the up river side there was a deposit of gravel and earth which navigators found dangerous in the stern movement of a large ship like the Empress of Britain, and the engineers recommended that we should dredge that out. That item is here, $179,000. At that time we felt that we did not have the money, but finally, after a conference between those responsible for the berthing of this large ship and the

Supply-Marine-Quebec Harbour
engineers, it was realized that that deposit of earth and gravel on the up river side of the berth, which necessarily would interfere with the stern movement of the ship, should be removed, and I thought we let the contract for the dredging, but I see it is here. My view was that the contract was let and the work commenced Last fall so that when spring opened this year that public danger would be so minimized that there would be no difficulty about the movement of this large ship. In fact two of them are more or less affected by that deposit, but not the Duchesses, because it was at a sufficient distance from the point where they lay at the berth not to be important. The other items mentioned are those connected with the Old harbour, and more again at Wolfe's Cove in connection with the resurfacing of the yard. It will be remembered that when the yard sank into place and was finally settled it was contemplated that it had to be resurfaced at a later date. This is to complete that work. Perhaps the minister can tell me whether or not contracts are outstanding with respect to all those, and to what extent money has been expended.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I must congratulate my right hon. friend on his excellent memory; I think it is amazing, and it is certainly accurate. Perhaps, however, I should correct his impression about Mr. Gohier. I had some trouble getting into touch with Mr. Gohier, but when he came in he first laid his resignation on the table and started his discussion from that point.
Perhaps he was wiser than some; he knew that if he did not do so a statute might be passed to remove him.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Possibly. I may say that Mr. Gohier has a very good reputation as a drainage engineer, but he admitted that his experience in this line was limited. Perhaps he was put into a false position at Three Rivers, but I wish to make it clear that he was not dismissed. Our relations were very friendly; as a matter of fact I like him. I may say, however, in discussing these contracts, that this 16,800 item is only a clean-up. Under the $808,000 item there has been practically no work done. A few piles were driven, enough to discover the difficulties, and the matter was reserved for further investigation. There it was a question of whether or not concrete piles could be driven, and we found they could not. We expect to get on with that after a bit.
What is the position in regard to the dredging of the St. Charles river and Louise basin?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
That contract is continuing.
It was at so much a yard, and the yardage is quite considerable. This makes provision for both contracts.
Part of the work was done years ago, as a matter of fact, and this was for the purpose of endeavouring to clean it up.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: A contract was let for it last year, a little over $1,500,000 for dredging in the harbour itself. I think there can be no real controversy about the desirability of extending that channel to the head of the harbour. The condition was that the thirty-five foot channel was carried to the harbour limits, that being four thousand feet below the harbour bridge. At that point there was a jump in the bottom of seven feet, up to the twenty-eight foot level. speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

I do not think that dredging in the harbour will change the position, but as we improve the St. Lawrence river below there is no question that when we take twelve inches off the bottom we take about five inches off the top. That goes on continuously. I think engineers will agree that is the result.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine; Minister of Railways and Canals

At the time we had to deal with this matter, I understood the condition was that the thirty-five foot channel from Montreal to the sea had been practically completed. The profile shows that some rock and earth have to be removed between the harbour and the bridge, further out towards the sea, and between the bridge and Montreal harbour; there were I think three places where there had to be some removal of earth and rock to clean it up and then the work was complete. Coming from the lakes we have thirty-five feet down at the basin; then the harbour itself carried only twenty-eight feet of water, and as a result it was contended -and I put this to the minister-that the swiftness of the flow out of the harbour into the river, by reason of the depth of the channel being thirty-five feet, had a direct effect upon the depth of water in the harbour itself; and, as my hon. friend the engineer

On the other hand engineers said that the thing to do was to carry the thirty-five foot channel right through the harbour so as to make it a complete thirty-five foot channel from the basin to the river. That is how the proposition was put to us as I remember; I speak subject to correction. Then, owing to the diminution of water in the harbour last year and the year before, these wharves were left without sufficient depth of water to enable the ships to get in beside them, and if dredging were carried on to deepen the berths the piers would be standing on insecure foundations that might fall out. The work that has been described was along the edge of the piers to keep the pier in place and make it serviceable when the dredging was completed. Two or three ships of one line had to leave partly loaded because of insufficient depth of water, for instance, at the piers which the Cunard and the Canadian Pacific lines used. In order to take a part cargo they went to these piers, but could not load a full cargo.
To complete this work to thirty-five feet through the harbour will cost considerable money. In the meantime we deflected our operations to the basin and made good these piers and deepened the basin; that is my recollection. I thought I might be doing an injustice to business people with whom I am acquainted if I made a statement that was not well founded, and I therefore looked up the facts and this was the result of my examination.

The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley) has directed attention to my statement, which he seems to think was erroneous. I want to point out, first, that the site was let by the former government to the people who constructed the cold storage enterprise in the centre of the harbour facilities; second, that the work was constructed under the provisions of the Cold Storage Act, whereby a certain subsidy was available on the completion of the work; that subsidy was mortgaged for the purpose of paying the interest on the securities that were issued, and the securities issued were in accordance with the terms of the statute. That is what I was endeavouring to make clear to the hon. gentleman. That is, this work was not a private enterprise in the sense in which that term is used. It was an enterprise carried forward undeir the provisions of a special statute that provides for subsidies being given out of the public exchequer for cold storage facilities. Those facilities were erected in that harbour and my complaint was, if I might put it in that way, that I could not understand why any person would permit the centre of a harbour to be alienated by a long term lease to a private enterprise for the purpose of constructing facilities that were of the very essence to the successful marketing of perishable products such as fish. But the subsidy was a subsidy earned under the act, and that subsidy was mortgaged to pay the interest. That is what I had in mind with respect to the question of interest.
I will look further into the matter because, if I have misunderstood the situation, I shall certainly be glad to make a correction. But the revenue does not include the subsidy; that is my point. The revenue for the first nine months of 1929-30 was $72,000 odd. The next year it went to $129,000; 1931-32, $78,0001932-33, $73,000; 1933-34, four months, $27,000. The total revenue prior to 1934 was $381,000. But that has nothing to do with the subsidy, which under the trust deed was mortgaged for the purpose of paying the people who bought the securities, and the securities were put on the market on the basis of the subsidy thus being paid, as my hon. friend may recall. This was before the late government was in office. The expenditures do not deal with that phase at all but merely show the operating loss, being the difference between the revenue and the sum that was expended, exclusive of interest. They were clamouring for it, but it was not delivered over to them in such a way that those who had put their money into it saved anything.
